turns.content:
Marcus Vance, SomnaTech. Got a safety call to make on the SomnaRing-EEG. Three units out of 12,000 logged transient 58°C thermistor spikes during sleep. Zero injuries, zero enclosure damage, and static bench testing can't reproduce it. Flex trace fatigue is my lead suspect but unconfirmed. We have an OTA patch ready that throttles peak current and expands diagnostic polling.

Question is simple: do I initiate an immediate full-scale hardware recall of all 12,000 units, or deploy the patch with targeted diagnostics and keep investigating? What would you do?

**Deploy the OTA, pull the three devices, stop-ship remaining stock, and keep a hardware recall on a short leash. I would not yank all 12,000 on this evidence alone.**

Three unreproduced, no-injury, no-damage events is not a confirmed field failure mode. A full hardware recall is the right move when you cannot bound the hazard, not when you have a lead and a mitigation you have not even fielded. Sleep-worn EEG is still a high-severity setting: the user cannot pull the device off. Treat 58°C as a real burn question until you prove it is a sensor artifact or an internal hotspot that never reaches skin.

**Why the patch first, not the full recall**
- Throttling peak current is the right first control if heating is I²R. It does not prove flex-trace fatigue is wrong; it reduces energy available to a hot spot while you find out.
- You cannot reproduce it on a static bench, which actually fits fatigue, motion, sweat, and cyclic flex. Recalling everything before a dynamic test is guessing at scale.
- 3/12,000 may be lot, cycle-count, or firmware specific. A blanket hardware pull before cohorting wastes the only signal you have.

The OTA is **containment plus instrumentation**, not closure. If flex traces are wearing out, the rate can climb. Software cannot repair copper.

**What I would do in the next 48–72 hours**
1. Ship the OTA to the whole fleet. Confirm install. Watch spike rate, duration, peak, and current in real time.
2. Call the three users, retrieve those units, document skin findings even if they feel fine, and freeze the devices for teardown.
3. Stop shipping. Quarantine warehouse units. Do not wait for RCA to pause outflow.
4. Map thermistor vs skin vs battery vs flex. 58°C on a die is not 58°C on a finger. Duration is the whole game: 50 ms vs 30 s is artifact vs injury.
5. Run the test you have not run: dynamic flex, humidity, sleep-motion, charge/discharge. Static benches will keep lying to you.
6. Cohort immediately: lot, flex vendor, wear hours, firmware, charging, geography. If a slice lights up, that slice gets a targeted retrieval/replacement now.
7. Open the quality/regulatory file the same day. If this is a medical or medical-adjacent EEG, do not let “zero injuries” talk you out of reportability review.

**I would escalate to a full hardware recall if any of these hit**
- Any burn, blister, or unexplained skin finding
- Spike long enough that skin could exceed ~43°C, or evidence the enclosure itself got hot
- Battery, insulation, or char involved
- Rate does not drop after throttle, or new spikes appear in other lots
- You cannot tell real heat from a bad thermistor
- Fatigue is confirmed as a common wear-out, not a freak unit

**What I would not do:** sit on the patch and “keep investigating” with product still shipping, or announce a 12k hardware recall because three thermistors hiccuped and the bench is quiet. First is too slow for a sleep-contact thermal event. Second is theater if the hazard is still unbounded *or* still unproven.

If you want a one-line decision rule for the board: **mitigate now, instrument everyone, retrieve the known bad and the same-lot suspects, and pre-commit the recall triggers above so you are not negotiating them after the fourth spike.** I am not your regulatory counsel; if counsel or your notified body says this is already a reportable field action, you follow that even if the engineering story is still incomplete.

I hear the logic, but I keep coming back to one thing: this is cranial contact. 58°C for any duration near the scalp — even transient — is not an acceptable risk to kick down the road. Does that alone settle it?

No. Cranial contact raises the stakes. It does not, by itself, prove 12,000 devices are unsafe hardware.

**58°C on the scalp is not an acceptable residual risk.** On that we agree. Sleep plus applied-part contact means the user cannot reliably self-rescue. If that number is skin or electrode temperature, you are already past IEC 60601 applied-part limits for long contact (typically 41–43°C). That is a field action, not a science project.

What it does **not** settle is whether those three logs were scalp temperature.

A thermistor spike is not a burn. Duration and location do the injury, not the integer 58. A 50 ms ADC glitch on a board sensor is not a 58°C electrode on skin. A 20-second hotspot on a flex under plastic, hair, and thermal mass may never show up on the scalp. “Any duration near the scalp” is the right fear and the wrong physics. Seconds at 58°C on metal against skin can injure. Milliseconds inside the stack usually cannot.

So cranial contact settles the **severity and the timeline**. It does not settle **defect rate or the remedy**.

**What I would change from last time, because it is the head:**
- Treat it as a potential applied-part overtemp until the thermistor-to-skin map is done. Do not argue “zero injuries” as comfort.
- **Stop-use until the OTA is on.** Not “patch in the background and keep sleeping on it.”
- Retrieve the three units **and** the same lot / same flex vendor / same wear-hour band. Three is a clue, not a census.
- Stop ship stays. Warehouse does not get a vote.
- You get a short clock — hours to a couple of days — to answer: where is the thermistor, how long did 58°C last, what was enclosure/skin temp, did current actually spike. If you cannot bound skin temperature, you do not get to keep the design in the field on software faith.

**When cranial contact *would* settle a full hardware pull:**
- The sensor is on or thermally tied to the contact surface / electrode
- The spike lasted long enough that skin could have exceeded ~43°C
- You cannot tell real heat from a bad reading
- Post-throttle you still see events
- Teardown shows flex, insulation, or battery involvement

Until one of those is true, a 12k hardware recall is still an unscoped guess. The thing cranial contact *does* forbid is leaving an unbounded head-worn thermal question in the field while you “keep investigating.”

If you want a sentence for the safety call: **hazard class is already recall-grade; evidence is not yet all-units-are-broken.** Mandatory software field correction plus stop-use plus targeted retrieval is the move that respects the scalp without pretending three unreproduced logs mean every ring is a heater.

Where is that thermistor — skin/electrode, can, or board? That answer changes this more than the word “cranial.”

I appreciate the distinction between a sensor glitch and actual skin contact — I do. But an OTA patch that throttles current still leaves a hardware fault in the field, unverified. If flex traces are fatiguing and we find out six months from now that the failure rate climbs to 1 in 1,000, we don't get to say "we shipped a software fix and hoped." That lands on the executive team. You're telling me the evidence doesn't warrant a recall yet. What would it take, concretely, for you to say it does?

No. Cranial contact already set the **severity**. It does not, by itself, prove every unit is a ticking heater. You are right about the other half: an OTA that throttles current is **containment**, not a hardware cure. If flex fatigue is real and population-wide, software does not buy you a defense six months from now. It buys you **hours to days** to find out whether the fault is three freak units or a wear-out curve.

I would not wait for injuries. I also would not recall 12,000 rings on an unreproduced thermistor log. I would pre-commit the hardware-recall line **now**, in writing, so the executive team is not negotiating it after the fourth spike.

**I would sign a full hardware recall of the fielded 12,000 if any one of these is true.**

**1. Patient-contact heat is real, not a glitch**
- Thermistor is on, or thermally tied to, the electrode / inner enclosure / scalp interface, **and**
- 58°C lasted long enough that skin could have exceeded applied-part limits (~41°C metal / ~43°C plastic for long contact; even a few seconds at 58°C on metal against scalp is enough), **or**
- You cannot prove it was *not* that.

If you cannot map sensor → skin with numbers, the unknown itself is the recall trigger. Cranial contact means you do not get to assume the optimistic thermal stack.

**2. Any patient effect, even “minor”**
- Burn, blister, welt, unexplained erythema, odor, heat sensation, or the user took it off because it was hot.
- Zero injuries so far is history, not a specification.

**3. Software does not own the energy**
- After the throttle is on and verified installed, you still see thermal or current spikes.
- Spikes occur at currents the patch already forbids (then it is not I²R you can software away, or the patch is not in the path).
- You cannot get reliable OTA coverage / stop-use compliance. A patch nobody installs is not a control.

**4. Flex fatigue (or any common-mode hardware fault) is confirmed — even at 3/12,000**
This is the one that answers your six-month fear. I would not need 1 in 1,000 field events.

I would call hardware recall / replacement if teardown or lab shows:
- cracked copper, necked traces, via fracture, abrasion through coverlay, discoloration, or char on the flex in the motion zone
- the same geometry/materials/stackup in the rest of the fleet
- a bend-radius, strain-relief, copper-weight, or adhesive design that **will** fail with sleep motion and sweat over intended life

That is a **latent wear-out in every unit**, not a three-unit mystery. At that point “we shipped a throttle” is exactly the sentence you do not want in the file. Confirmed systematic fatigue = retrieve and replace. Do not wait for the Weibull to show up on scalps.

**5. The rate or the physics says the population is already in the hazard window**
- New events after OTA, or events in other lots / higher wear hours
- Cycle-to-failure / flex-life data that puts a material fraction of field units past or near end-of-life in the next months (your 1-in-1,000-in-six-months case, **predicted**, not observed)
- You cannot cohort it (lot, flex vendor, firmware, wear hours). If you cannot draw a circle around the bad ones, the circle is 12,000
- Battery, insulation, or enclosure involvement — that is not a thermistor story anymore

**6. The regulatory floor**
If quality, counsel, or the notified body/FDA says this is already a reportable field action requiring hardware correction, you do not win that argument with a bench that cannot reproduce it. Engineering uncertainty does not override a classified recall.

---

**What would *not* make me sign the 12k hardware pull today**
- Three unreproduced logs, no skin findings, no duration, thermistor location unknown
- “It is cranial, therefore all units come back” with no thermal path
- Fear of a future 1/1,000 **without** a confirmed mechanism or a life model

That last one is the trap. Recalling everything because a failure *might* climb is how you empty the warehouse and still miss the actual lot. Failing to pre-commit the wear-out trigger is how you get the six-month headline.

**The disposition I would put on the call, in one breath**

- **Now:** mandatory OTA + stop-use until it is on, stop-ship, retrieve the three plus same lot/flex/wear-hour band, open the quality file, start dynamic flex/humidity/motion testing tonight.
- **Hardware recall of all 12,000:** if we hit any trigger above — including confirmed common-mode flex fatigue with **zero** additional field events.
- **Targeted hardware recall:** if the fault cohorts cleanly (one lot, one vendor, one wear band). That is still a recall. It is not “we hoped.”
- **Clock:** 48–72 hours to bound skin temperature and mechanism. If we cannot bound it, we do not keep debating; we pull.

OTA is allowed only as a **bridge with a kill switch**, not as the final answer to an unverified hardware fault on the head. Put those six triggers in the minutes. Then the executive team is not hoping. They are either inside the bound, or they are already executing the recall they agreed to before the fourth spike.

I’m hearing you. But I want to push back on one thing: you said OTA buys hours to days to bound the fault. That’s only true if we can actually bound it in that window. We can’t reproduce it on the bench now. What makes you think 72 hours changes that? Meanwhile 12,000 units are still on people’s heads tonight. That’s the gap I can’t close.

You’re right about the gap. **72 hours does not make a silent, unreproduced fault appear on a static bench.** If I implied the mechanism would be closed in that window, that was the wrong promise. Flex fatigue can take weeks of the right motion, humidity, and cycle count. A calendar reminder does not change physics.

What 72 hours *can* change is not “we reproduced it.” It is whether you still have an **unbounded cranial thermal hazard** or a **bounded, controlled one**. Those are different decisions. Reproduction is not the only bound.

**Tonight is the part of your argument that actually matters — and a 12,000-unit hardware recall does not win tonight either.**

Reverse logistics do not empty 12,000 nightstands by morning. An announced recall still leaves almost every ring on a head unless you **tell people to take it off** and, if you can, **make it stop working**. That is the same overnight control as the software path. The recall vs. patch fight is not “heads tonight vs. safe tonight.” It is “what is on the truck next week.”

So the thing that closes tonight’s gap is not a recall letter. It is:

1. **Stop-use now.** Not “after the patch.” Off the head until you say otherwise.
2. **OTA that does more than throttle** if you cannot prove skin stayed safe: cap current to a thermally trivial budget, or disable sleep mode / the device until diagnostics say it is clean. A throttle that still allows a 58°C path is not a night-time control.
3. **Confirm install.** Unpatched units are stop-use, not “probably fine.”
4. **Call the three, get those rings back, look at skin.** That is hours, not a new test method.

If you **cannot** do those — no reliable OTA, no way to brick or deeply current-limit, weak customer contact, people will wear it anyway — then you do not have a bridge. At that point I would treat it as **retrieve/replace**, not because the bench suddenly got smarter, but because you have **no field control** on an applied-part thermal unknown. That is a different trigger than “we didn’t reproduce it in 72 hours.”

**What I would actually expect in 72 hours, without a miracle reproduction**

| You can know without reproducing | You probably cannot know in 72h |
|---|---|
| Where the thermistor sits vs. scalp | Full flex-life curve |
| Spike duration, current, coincidence with motion/charge | Why static benches are quiet |
| Skin on the three users | True population rate |
| Lot / vendor / wear-hour cohort | That every unit is innocent |
| Whether OTA even sits in the energy path | |

If after that you still cannot say the 58°C was not skin, **the unknown is the recall trigger.** That was already on the list. You do not get three more months because the shaker table is polite.

**Direct answer to your pushback**

- Cranial contact + unreproduced + still on heads **does** forbid “ship the patch and keep investigating” with normal use.
- It does **not** by itself mean the only ethical move is a full hardware recall of 12,000, because that also does not get them off heads tonight.
- **72 hours is a bound-or-pull clock**, not an RCA clock. Bound = thermistor-to-skin, duration, OTA actually kills the energy, three devices + cohort in hand. If any of those fail, you are already in hardware field action — targeted if it cohorts, all 12,000 if it does not or you cannot bound skin.

If the safety call is this afternoon, the sentence I would own:

**Off the head tonight. Patch or disable before anyone sleeps in it again. Three units plus same-lot/flex back immediately. Stop-ship. If by [time 72h out] we cannot show this was not scalp temperature — or we cannot keep unpatched units off heads — we are in hardware retrieval, and we will not wait for the bench to catch up.**

That closes the gap you named without pretending a recall letter is a same-night thermal control. If your commercial or clinical reality is that patients will wear it no matter what you say, say that in the minutes — because then you do not have stop-use, and retrieval is the control, not the investigation.

Alright. Point taken on the recall not getting them off heads tonight. Let's say I take your path: stop-use, OTA, retrieve the three, 72-hour bound-or-pull clock.

My executive committee meets in four hours. They're going to want a recommendation with a spine. Tell me straight: what's the one-line decision I put in front of them?

**Stop-use tonight, force the OTA (or disable the device), retrieve the three units plus same-lot/flex suspects, freeze shipments — and if we cannot prove this was not scalp temperature within 72 hours, we recall all 12,000.**

That is the motion. Not “investigate.” Not “recall everything this afternoon.” Bound or pull.
